Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Kwame, age 55, was mixing pigments in the back of the community studio when his younger brother collapsed near the easels. The death was sudden and unheralded, an unexpected cardiac event that left his brother breathless before the ambulance sirens wailed through the open doors. His African-American background had prepared him for many things, but the silence that followed the paramedics’ efforts was absolute. Kwame’s memories of that afternoon are sharp photographs: the spilled turpentine, the white canvas sheet pulled over his brother’s face, the red and blue lights cutting through the workshop windows. He still carries these visual memories, and when he remembers the event, he feels overwhelming grief, a heavy wave that settles in his chest. On other days, the full emotional intensity of that loss floods him without any clear image, just a raw, unmoored pressure that requires no picture to be felt. In the weeks that followed, Kwame found himself braced. He was certain that the workplace, where they had shared a decade of canvases and quiet conversations, now held the same quiet threat. He stopped returning to the studio on the days when his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger. When people talked about losing loved ones, Kwame would step back, listening to the stories as though they were unfolding in his own room. The sight and sound of ambulances on the street drew him outside or made his shoulders rise. He had come to believe that if he did not stay watchful, he might miss the warning signs in his own surroundings. Sleep grew harder. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day. The studio’s overhead lights felt like a promise of order, but the dark outside his bedroom window invited a low, persistent hum of watchfulness. Even inside his own home, he felt on guard, listening to the floorboards, the refrigerator, the distant traffic, treating them as potential signals rather than background noise. His body remained constantly tense, and the night vigilance settled into his posture without him consciously deciding to hold it there. Over the months, these states accumulated and altered his daily rhythm. He stopped accepting gallery invitations, and his wife noticed how he lingered at the door rather than stepping out. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the sense that his life had been destroyed by the trauma. He felt like he didn’t know himself anymore, a man who once measured time by brushstrokes and drying paint, now measuring it by heartbeats and distant sirens. He felt isolated and set apart from others, watching couples laugh at dinners, certain that their easy rhythms belonged to a different world. The occupational consequence was concrete: he began painting at home, stretching long hours to avoid the workplace trigger, and missed commissions accumulated alongside them. His wife learned to speak softly when passing the window where he stood, watching the street. His self-reported symptoms clustered around him like a carefully managed perimeter. A recent clinical assessment placed his score at sixty-seven, a number that mirrored what he described in session. It was the slow narrowing of his world, the way his painted rooms began to feel like a sealed boundary, that finally brought him to seek help. He sits now ready to face the work ahead, most hoping to reclaim the studio without losing the peace he has fought for, and most afraid of the quiet that follows when the lights go down.
